questions.q: Which clause runs first, conceptually, in a SELECT statement's logical processing order?
options: FROM
SELECT
ORDER BY
HAVING
questions.explain: Logical query processing evaluates FROM/JOIN first, then WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY — even though SELECT is written first, it isn't evaluated first.

questions.q: What does SELECT DISTINCT do?
options: Removes duplicate rows from the result set
Removes duplicate column names
Sorts the result set
Selects only the first row
questions.explain: DISTINCT compares entire result rows and removes exact duplicates after the SELECT list is evaluated.

questions.q: Why can't you use an aggregate function like COUNT() or AVG() directly in a WHERE clause?
options: WHERE filters rows before aggregation happens, so aggregate results don't exist yet
WHERE only accepts string comparisons
Aggregates are only allowed in ORDER BY
SQL Server doesn't support aggregate functions at all
questions.explain: WHERE filters individual rows before GROUP BY runs; use HAVING to filter after aggregation, once group-level values exist.

questions.q: By default, how does ORDER BY sort a column of dates?
options: Ascending, oldest date first
Descending, newest date first
Alphabetically by month name
Randomly unless a seed is specified
questions.explain: ASC is the default sort direction in SQL Server; oldest dates sort first unless DESC is specified.

questions.q: A LEFT JOIN between Customers and Orders returns a customer with no orders. What appears in the Orders columns for that row?
options: NULL
An empty string
The row is excluded from the result
questions.explain: LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table; when there's no matching row on the right, SQL Server fills the right table's columns with NULL rather than dropping the row.

questions.q: What does a CROSS JOIN between a 5-row table and a 3-row table produce?
options: 15 rows — every combination of rows from both tables
8 rows — the tables concatenated
3 rows — the smaller table's row count
An error, since CROSS JOIN requires a join condition
questions.explain: CROSS JOIN has no join condition — it returns the Cartesian product, every row from the first table paired with every row from the second (5 × 3 = 15).

questions.q: You write SELECT CustomerId, COUNT(*) FROM Orders GROUP BY CustomerId. Why would adding OrderDate to the SELECT list, without adding it to GROUP BY, cause an error in SQL Server?
options: Every non-aggregated column in SELECT must also appear in GROUP BY, since SQL Server can't know which OrderDate value represents the group
OrderDate is a reserved keyword
GROUP BY only allows one column total
COUNT(*) can only be used with a single grouping column
questions.explain: Once you GROUP BY CustomerId, each row in the result represents many underlying rows — SQL Server requires every selected column to be either in GROUP BY or wrapped in an aggregate, so it always knows which single value to show.

questions.q: What's the key difference between CAST and CONVERT when converting a datetime to a string in SQL Server?
options: CONVERT accepts an optional style code to control date formatting; CAST does not
CAST only works on numbers; CONVERT only works on dates
They produce different data types
CONVERT is deprecated in favor of CAST
questions.explain: Both convert between data types, but CONVERT takes a third, style-code argument (e.g. 101 for mm/dd/yyyy) that lets you control exactly how a date renders as a string — CAST has no such option.

questions.q: In T-SQL, what does the expression WHERE MiddleName = NULL actually do?
options: Returns zero rows, because NULL can't be compared with = — you must use IS NULL
Returns every row where MiddleName is empty
Returns every row where MiddleName is NULL
Causes a syntax error
questions.explain: NULL represents "unknown," so any = comparison against NULL evaluates to unknown, not true — the row is never returned. IS NULL is the correct, and only, way to test for NULL.

questions.q: What makes a subquery "correlated" rather than a plain subquery?
options: It references a column from the outer query, so it re-runs once per outer row
It returns more than one row
It uses a JOIN instead of WHERE
It's written using a CTE instead of parentheses
questions.explain: A correlated subquery reaches back into the outer query's current row (e.g. WHERE o.CustomerId = c.CustomerId) — because of that reference, SQL Server conceptually evaluates it once per outer row, rather than once total.

questions.q: What two parts does a recursive CTE require?
options: An anchor member and a recursive member combined with UNION ALL
A WHILE loop and a cursor
A self-join and a HAVING clause
Two separate CTEs joined together
questions.explain: A recursive CTE always has an anchor query (the starting rows) UNION ALL'd with a recursive query that references the CTE's own name, repeating until it returns no more rows.

questions.q: Can a scalar user-defined function in SQL Server perform an INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE?
options: No — functions can't modify data or have other side effects, only return a value
Yes, but only inside a transaction
Yes, if it's marked SCHEMABINDING
Yes, but only against temp tables
questions.explain: SQL Server functions are restricted to being side-effect-free — they can only compute and return a value, never modify database state. Stored procedures are for that.

questions.q: What's the main practical difference between a local temp table (#Temp) and a table variable (@Temp)?
options: Table variables have narrower transaction/logging behavior and are scoped to the batch/procedure; #Temp tables can persist for the whole session across batches
They're functionally identical
Table variables can hold more rows than temp tables
#Temp tables can't have indexes
questions.explain: Both live in tempdb, but a table variable's scope is tied to the batch/procedure it's declared in and it interacts differently with transactions and statistics, while a local temp table persists for the life of the session and can be shared across batches within it.

questions.q: What does SET XACT_ABORT ON do inside a stored procedure with a TRY/CATCH block?
options: Forces SQL Server to fully roll back the transaction automatically on a runtime error, rather than leaving it in an uncommittable state
Aborts the procedure immediately with no CATCH block running
Disables all error handling
Commits the transaction automatically regardless of errors
questions.explain: Without XACT_ABORT, some errors leave a transaction open but doomed (uncommittable) even inside CATCH. XACT_ABORT ON guarantees SQL Server rolls the whole transaction back on error, which is why it's paired with TRY/CATCH in production code.

questions.q: A query needs to rank sales reps by revenue, but ties should share the same rank with no gaps in the numbering afterward. Which window function fits?
options: DENSE_RANK
ROW_NUMBER
RANK
NTILE
questions.explain: RANK() leaves gaps after ties (1,1,3), ROW_NUMBER() never ties at all, and DENSE_RANK() is the one that gives tied rows the same rank with no gap in the sequence that follows (1,1,2).

questions.q: A WHERE clause reads WHERE YEAR(OrderDate) = 2024. Why does this typically prevent SQL Server from doing an efficient index seek on OrderDate?
options: Wrapping the column in a function makes the predicate non-SARGable, forcing a scan instead of a seek
YEAR() is not a valid function in WHERE clauses
OrderDate must be indexed as an INT to work with YEAR()
SQL Server caches YEAR() results so it's actually faster
questions.explain: Applying a function to the indexed column (rather than to the comparison value) makes the predicate non-SARGable — SQL Server can't use the index's sort order and has to evaluate YEAR(OrderDate) row by row, i.e. scan.

questions.q: An execution plan shows an Index Seek followed by a Key Lookup for the same query. What does that combination usually indicate?
options: The index used isn't a covering index — SQL Server had to go back to the clustered index to fetch columns not included in it
The query has a syntax error
The table has no clustered index at all
The query is already fully optimized
questions.explain: A Key Lookup means the nonclustered index seek found the right rows but didn't include every column the query needs, so SQL Server does an extra lookup per row into the clustered index — a sign the index isn't "covering" and could be improved with an INCLUDE.

questions.q: What's the main purpose of a foreign key constraint?
options: It enforces that a value in the child table must exist in the referenced parent table, preventing orphaned rows
It automatically creates an index on the column
It encrypts the column's data
It's purely documentation and has no runtime effect
questions.explain: A foreign key is a real, enforced constraint — SQL Server rejects an INSERT or UPDATE that would leave a child row pointing at a parent value that doesn't exist, which is what keeps referential integrity intact.

questions.q: Why use a surrogate key (e.g. an IDENTITY int) instead of a natural key (e.g. an email address) as a table's primary key?
options: Natural keys can change over time or turn out not to be as unique as assumed, breaking every foreign key that references them
Surrogate keys are required by the SQL standard
Natural keys can't be indexed
Surrogate keys make JOINs impossible
questions.explain: A "unique" natural value like an email or SSN can still change, be reused, or turn out to collide — a surrogate key is immune to those real-world data problems because it has no business meaning of its own.

questions.q: In a star schema, what's stored in the fact table versus the dimension tables?
options: The fact table holds measurable events/metrics and foreign keys to dimensions; dimension tables hold the descriptive attributes for filtering and grouping
The fact table holds descriptive text; dimensions hold only numbers
There's no difference — both store the same columns
Dimension tables always have more rows than the fact table
questions.explain: The fact table is the narrow, tall table of numeric measures (e.g. SalesAmount) plus foreign keys, while each dimension table (Date, Product, Customer) supplies the descriptive columns you slice and filter by — that separation is the defining shape of a star schema.
